summary: Describes the ITU-T H.350 series of Recommendations for directory service architectures that support multimedia conferencing. The goal is to "directory enable" video and voice conferencing so it can use existing identity management and enterprise directories.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of keeping a separate phone book for video calls, this lets video calling look people up in the one directory a company already has.

questions: how do h.350 and ldap work together
subtitle: Unified directory for multimedia conferencing endpoints.

tldr.problem: Organizations that deploy video and voice conferencing endpoints need a way to integrate them with existing enterprise directories instead of maintaining separate systems for each protocol or vendor.
tldr.mechanism: H.350 defines a standard LDAP schema with object classes (commObject and commURI) that represent endpoints and associate them with users, allowing multiple vendors' systems to read from a single source.
tldr.outcome: Enterprise directories can now serve as the canonical source for endpoint information, reducing duplication and allowing white pages searches and click-to-dial features to work across different conferencing systems.

facts.label: Supported protocols
facts.value: H.323, H.235, H.320, SIP, and others

today: RFC 3944 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the basis for H.350-compliant deployments, though adoption of H.350 for directory integration varies by vendor.

sections.title: Why Unified Directory Services
sections.content:
Organizations deploying video and voice conferencing face a complex problem: multiple vendors' systems and protocols each require their own directory or configuration, duplicating user and endpoint information. H.350 solves this by defining a standardized LDAP schema that lets H.323, H.235, H.320 and SIP systems all share the same directory.

The goal is to 'directory enable' multimedia conferencing by integrating with existing enterprise directories (systems like Active Directory or OpenLDAP that manage user accounts). Without standardization, administrators must maintain separate configurations for each protocol and vendor, increasing risk of data inconsistency and slowing deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: When a company uses video phones from different makers, each one has its own phone book. H.350 is like a master phone book that all of them can read from.

sections.title: The Two-Way Pointer Model
sections.content:
H.350 uses two linked object classes to connect users to endpoints. The commURI attribute is added to a user's directory entry and contains an LDAP URL pointing to one or more commObject entries that represent the user's conferencing devices (IP phone, video endpoint, etc.). The commOwner attribute in the commObject points back to the user or resource that owns it.

This design is non-invasive: only the simple commURI object class is added to existing user entries, while endpoint information can be stored in a separate directory or the same one. A user can have multiple commURI pointers (e.g., a desktop video system and a phone), and each can point to a different directory operated by a different service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The user's entry has a link that says 'my video phone is over here,' and the video phone entry has a link back that says 'I belong to this person.' They point at each other.

sections.title: Object Classes and Attributes
sections.content:
The commObject class is the core structural object class that represents a conferencing endpoint. It requires a commUniqueId attribute to identify the endpoint uniquely within its directory, and optionally includes commOwner (to name the user or resource) and commPrivate (a boolean for privacy, like an unlisted number).

Auxiliary classes extend commObject to add protocol-specific attributes. H.350.4 defines SIPIdentity, which adds attributes like SIPIdentitySIPURI (the SIP address like sip:alice@example.com), SIPIdentityRegistrarAddress (server address), SIPIdentityUserName and SIPIdentityPassword (for authentication). Endpoints can include multiple auxiliary classes to support multiple protocols simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint needs an ID number and an owner. Different types of endpoints (SIP phones, H.323 systems, etc.) add their own extra fields to describe how to reach them.

sections.title: Extensibility and Implementation
sections.content:
H.350 allows implementations to extend the schema by subclassing existing object classes or creating auxiliary classes with additional attributes. For example, an implementation might add billing codes or model numbers. Extensions must not break compatibility with the base specification.

The RFC provides LDIF (LDAP Data Interchange Format) configuration examples for adding the schema to an LDAP server. An optional indexing profile recommends which attributes should be indexed for performance (e.g., commUniqueId for equality searches, commOwner for presence queries).
sections.plainLanguage: Different organizations can add their own custom fields if needed, as long as they don't break the standard parts. The RFC explains how to set up the directory server to handle this efficiently.

sections.title: Security and Directory Access
sections.content:
H.350 does not alter the security models of the underlying protocols (H.323, SIP, etc.) but provides a standardized place to store credentials. SIP authentication credentials can be stored (H.350.4 includes SIPIdentityPassword), and S/MIME certificates can be stored via the userSMIMECertificate attribute for encryption and integrity.

The RFC recommends that call servers and H.350 directories mutually authenticate before exchanging information, and that communications use secure channels like TLS. Administrators are advised to set access control lists carefully: password attributes should be restricted to the authenticated user, while address attributes might be public. These access control details are a matter of site policy, not the standard itself.
sections.plainLanguage: If the directory stores passwords, it becomes a target for attack, so it needs strong security. Addresses can be public, like a real phone book, but passwords need protection.
